questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The liverwort Marchantia bears small cups on the upper surface of its thallus. Each cup contains green, multicellular buds that are washed out by rain and grow into new plants. What are these buds, and what kind of reproduction is this?
options: B) Spores; sexual reproduction after meiosis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gemmae; asexual reproduction.
Why: Liverworts reproduce asexually by fragmentation of the thallus or by gemmae. Gemmae are green, multicellular asexual buds formed in small cups called gemma cups. They detach and each grows into a new plant that is genetically the same as the parent. No gametes or meiosis are involved.
Why not the others: (B) Spores are formed by meiosis inside the capsule of the sporophyte, not in cups on the thallus. (C) A zygote is formed by fusion of gametes inside the archegonium. (D) Bryophytes do not form seeds.
Key point: Gemma cups on Marchantia: asexual reproduction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The diagram shows five united sepals, five free petals, five stamens and two fused carpels. Use the longitudinal section to infer ovary position. Which floral formula matches both views? Here brackets denote fusion.
options: A) K5 C(5) A5 G(2) inferior
B) K(5) C5 A5 G(2) superior
C) K(5) C5 A(5) G2 superior
D) K5 C5 A5 G2 inferior
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) K(5) C5 A5 G(2) superior.
Why: In a floral formula, brackets show fusion. Five united sepals are K(5); five free petals are C5; five free stamens are A5; two fused carpels are G(2). The longitudinal section shows the other parts attached below the ovary, so the ovary is superior (written with a line under G).
Why not the others: (A) puts the brackets on the petals and leaves them off the sepals, and makes the ovary inferior. (C) shows the stamens as united and the carpels as free. (D) shows nothing as fused and the ovary as inferior.
Key point: K calyx, C corolla, A androecium, G gynoecium; ( ) = fused.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Quiescent (G₀) stage of the cell cycle
questions.question: Heart muscle cells of an adult mammal are metabolically active but do not divide. In which stage of the cell cycle are they?
options: A) S phase, with DNA replication going on
B) G₂ phase, about to enter mitosis
C) The quiescent stage (G₀), after leaving G₁
D) Metaphase, with chromosomes held at the equator
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The quiescent stage (G₀), after leaving G₁.
Why: Cells that do not divide leave the cycle from G₁ and enter an inactive stage called G₀. They stay alive and carry out their normal work, but they do not replicate DNA or divide unless called on to do so. Heart muscle cells and many nerve cells of an adult are in this state.
Why not the others: (A) Cells in S phase are copying their DNA in preparation for division. (B) Cells in G₂ have already doubled their DNA and go on to mitosis. (D) Metaphase is a stage of mitosis itself.
Key point: G₀: metabolically active, not dividing.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In bright light with closed stomata, a C3 leaf shows net CO₂ uptake falling sharply, while a C4 leaf retains appreciable uptake at the same temperature. Which explanation best fits the contrast?
options: A) C4 plants never use RuBisCO
B) C3 plants cannot make ATP under bright light
C) C4 mesophyll lacks any oxygen
D) C4 CO₂ concentration in bundle-sheath cells suppresses RuBisCO oxygenation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C4 CO₂ concentration in bundle-sheath cells suppresses RuBisCO oxygenation.
Why: With stomata closed, the CO₂ inside a C₃ leaf falls and O₂ builds up, so RuBisCO binds more O₂ and photorespiration wastes fixed carbon. A C₄ leaf first fixes CO₂ with PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll and releases it in the bundle-sheath cells, where RuBisCO works at a high CO₂ concentration and hardly reacts with O₂.
Why not the others: (A) C₄ plants do use RuBisCO, in the bundle-sheath cells. (B) Bright light increases ATP production. (C) Mesophyll cells of C₄ plants do contain oxygen.
Key point: C₄ plants concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO and avoid photorespiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A heart pumps 5 L min⁻¹ into a systemic circuit whose effective mean pressure drop is 100 mm Hg. If flow stays 5 L min⁻¹ but vascular resistance falls by 20%, what pressure drop is required in the same linear-flow approximation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 80 mm Hg.
Given: Flow = 5 L min⁻¹ in both cases; pressure drop = 100 mm Hg; resistance falls by 20%.
Formula/Principle: Pressure drop = flow × resistance.
Step 1: New resistance = 0.80 × old resistance.
Step 2: Flow is unchanged, so the pressure drop changes in the same ratio as the resistance.
Step 3: New pressure drop = 0.80 × 100 = 80 mm Hg.
Why: For a steady flow, the pressure needed is proportional to the resistance of the vessels, much as voltage is proportional to resistance at a fixed current. Widening of the arterioles lowers resistance, so the same output needs less pressure.
Why not the others: (B) 100 mm Hg ignores the change in resistance. (C) 120 mm Hg raises the pressure by 20% instead of lowering it. (D) 64 mm Hg applies the 20% reduction twice.
Key point: ΔP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In an apple, the fleshy part that is eaten does not come from the ovary wall. From which part of the flower does it develop, and what is such a fruit called?
options: A) The ovule; a true fruit
B) The thalamus; a false fruit
C) The style; a parthenocarpic fruit
D) The petals; a true fruit
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The thalamus; a false fruit.
Why: In most plants the fruit develops only from the ovary and is called a true fruit. In apple, strawberry and cashew the thalamus (the swollen end of the flower stalk) also grows and forms the main edible part. Such fruits are called false fruits; the true fruit of the apple is the core that holds the seeds.
Why not the others: (A) The ovule becomes the seed, not the flesh. (C) The style withers after fertilisation; a parthenocarpic fruit is one formed without fertilisation, such as banana. (D) Petals fall off after fertilisation.
Key point: True fruit: from the ovary only. False fruit: thalamus also contributes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Human skin colour shows a continuous range from very dark to very light instead of a few distinct classes. Which pattern of inheritance explains this?
options: A) A single gene with one dominant and one recessive allele
B) A single gene with two codominant alleles
C) Three or more genes, each with an additive effect on the same character
D) One gene affecting several unrelated characters
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Three or more genes, each with an additive effect on the same character.
Why: A character controlled by several genes is polygenic. Each dominant allele adds a little to the character, so the phenotype depends on how many dominant alleles are present. With three gene pairs (A, B, C) there can be from zero to six dominant alleles, which gives many shades between the two extremes.
Why not the others: (A) One gene with dominance gives only two classes. (B) Two codominant alleles of one gene give three classes. (D) One gene affecting several characters is pleiotropy.
Key point: Polygenic trait: many genes, additive effect, continuous variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A virus infects host cells, and extracellular viral particles are neutralised by serum antibodies while already infected cells remain. Which additional response most directly removes those infected cells?
options: A) Plasma cells releasing more neutralising antibody
B) Complement acting only on free virions
C) Memory B cells without effector activation
D) Cytotoxic T cells recognising antigen displayed by infected cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cytotoxic T cells recognising antigen displayed by infected cells.
Why: Antibodies work in body fluids: they bind free virus particles but cannot reach virus inside a cell. Infected cells display fragments of viral protein on their surface. Cytotoxic (killer) T cells recognise these and destroy the cell, which removes the place where the virus multiplies. This is cell-mediated immunity.
Why not the others: (A) More antibody still cannot enter infected cells. (B) Complement acting on free virus does nothing to cells already infected. (C) Memory cells that are not activated carry out no attack.
Key point: Antibodies: free pathogens. Cytotoxic T cells: infected cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A plasmid has intact marker S and a cloning site inside marker R. After ligation, colonies grow on S-antibiotic; a colony fails on R-antibiotic. Which control most directly tests whether failure is due to insertion at R rather than a nonrecombinant vector's ordinary phenotype?
options: A) Transform and plate an uncut parent vector on both antibiotics
B) Repeat only the same S plate without a vector control
C) Measure colony diameter without changing selection
D) Sequence an unrelated chromosomal gene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Transform and plate an uncut parent vector on both antibiotics.
Why: A control changes only the factor being tested. The uncut parent vector has both markers intact, so cells carrying it should grow on both antibiotics. If they do, then a colony that grows on the S antibiotic but not on the R antibiotic must have lost R through the insert, and not through some ordinary property of the vector or the host.
Why not the others: (B) Repeating the same plate gives no comparison. (C) Colony size says nothing about which genes work. (D) An unrelated chromosomal gene is not connected with the plasmid markers.
Key point: A control differs from the test in one factor only.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Plants have gross production 10000 kJ and respiration 4000 kJ over the measured interval. Herbivores A and B assimilate 2000 and 1000 kJ and respire 1400 and 700 kJ respectively. A predator consumes one half of A's new production and two thirds of B's, assimilates 80% of that food energy and respires 250 kJ. The diagram shows these routes. What fraction of plant net primary production becomes new predator biomass?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/40.
Given: Plants: GPP 10 000 kJ, respiration 4000 kJ. Herbivore A: assimilates 2000, respires 1400. Herbivore B: assimilates 1000, respires 700. Predator eats 1/2 of A's production and 2/3 of B's, assimilates 80%, respires 250 kJ.
Formula/Principle: Production (new biomass) = energy assimilated − respiration.
Step 1: Plant NPP = 10 000 − 4000 = 6000 kJ.
Step 2: Production of A = 2000 − 1400 = 600 kJ; of B = 1000 − 700 = 300 kJ.
Step 3: Predator eats 600/2 + 300 × 2/3 = 300 + 200 = 500 kJ and assimilates 0.80 × 500 = 400 kJ.
Step 4: Predator production = 400 − 250 = 150 kJ; fraction = 150/6000 = 1/40.
Why: At every step only part of the energy is eaten, only part of that is assimilated, and most of the assimilated energy is lost as heat in respiration. Only what is left is stored as new biomass, which is why so little reaches the higher trophic levels.
Why not the others: (A) 1/15 uses the 400 kJ assimilated, before respiration. (C) 1/12 uses the 500 kJ eaten. (D) 1/10 is the rule-of-thumb transfer for a single step.
Key point: Production = assimilation − respiration, at every level.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At a locus, measured allele frequencies are p=0.7 and q=0.3. Observed genotype frequencies are AA=0.60, Aa=0.20, aa=0.20. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A) The allele frequencies cannot be 0.7 and 0.3
B) The genotype frequencies exactly match Hardy–Weinberg proportions
C) The genotype frequencies depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions despite matching the stated allele frequencies
D) Heterozygotes must have frequency 0.49 at equilibrium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The genotype frequencies depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions despite matching the stated allele frequencies.
Given: Observed AA = 0.60, Aa = 0.20, aa = 0.20; stated p = 0.7, q = 0.3.
Formula/Principle: p = f(AA) + ½f(Aa). At equilibrium the genotypes are p², 2pq, q².
Step 1: p = 0.60 + 0.10 = 0.70 and q = 0.20 + 0.10 = 0.30, so the allele frequencies agree.
Step 2: Expected at equilibrium: AA = 0.49, Aa = 0.42, aa = 0.09.
Step 3: Observed heterozygotes (0.20) are far fewer than expected (0.42).
Why: Allele frequencies alone do not tell how the alleles are paired. A shortage of heterozygotes with an excess of both homozygotes suggests non-random mating, such as inbreeding, or a mixture of separate populations.
Why not the others: (A) The observed genotypes do give p = 0.7 and q = 0.3. (B) 0.60, 0.20, 0.20 are not 0.49, 0.42, 0.09. (D) 0.49 is the expected frequency of AA, not of the heterozygote.
Key point: First find p and q from the genotypes, then compare with p², 2pq, q².

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A few birds are blown by a storm to a distant island and start a new population. After some generations the allele frequencies there differ greatly from those of the mainland population, although the island and the mainland have similar environments. What is the most likely cause?
options: A) Directed mutation caused by the new habitat
B) Stabilising selection for the mainland type
C) Gene flow from the mainland
D) The founder effect, a form of genetic drift
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The founder effect, a form of genetic drift.
Why: A small group that starts a new population carries only a sample of the alleles of the original population, and by chance the sample may be very unrepresentative. The new population keeps these altered frequencies. Because the environments are similar, selection is unlikely to be the cause; the change is due to chance, which is genetic drift.
Why not the others: (A) Mutations are random and are not directed by the habitat. (B) Stabilising selection for the mainland type would keep the frequencies similar, not make them different. (C) Gene flow from the mainland would make the two populations more alike.
Key point: Few founders → chance change in allele frequencies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Direction of gas exchange in the lungs
questions.question: Typical partial pressures are: alveolar air, O₂ 104 mm Hg and CO₂ 40 mm Hg; deoxygenated blood entering the lungs, O₂ 40 mm Hg and CO₂ 45 mm Hg. In which directions do the two gases move across the alveolar wall?
options: A) Both gases move from the blood into the alveoli
B) Both gases move from the alveoli into the blood
C) O₂ moves from blood to alveoli; CO₂ from alveoli to blood
D) O₂ moves from alveoli to blood; CO₂ from blood to alveoli
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) O₂ moves from alveoli to blood; CO₂ from blood to alveoli.
Why: Gases diffuse from a region of higher partial pressure to one of lower partial pressure, and each gas follows its own gradient. For O₂ the gradient is from alveolar air (104 mm Hg) to blood (40 mm Hg). For CO₂ it is from blood (45 mm Hg) to alveolar air (40 mm Hg). The CO₂ gradient is small, but CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble than O₂, so it still diffuses quickly.
Why not the others: (A) O₂ cannot move from 40 to 104 mm Hg. (B) CO₂ cannot move from 40 to 45 mm Hg. (C) has both gases moving against their gradients.
Key point: Each gas diffuses down its own partial-pressure gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which protein is the most abundant in the animal world, and which is the most abundant in the whole biosphere?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Collagen; RuBisCO.
Why: Collagen is the structural protein of connective tissue, such as tendons, skin, cartilage and bone, and is the most abundant protein in animals. RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is the enzyme that fixes CO₂ in all green plants and algae, and is the most abundant protein in the biosphere.
Why not the others: (B) Haemoglobin is confined to red blood cells and insulin is a hormone made in tiny amounts. (C) has the two answers the wrong way round. (D) Keratin is plentiful in hair and nails but less so than collagen, and trypsin is a digestive enzyme.
Key point: Animal world: collagen. Biosphere: RuBisCO.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Species-area exponent and changed habitat coefficient
questions.question: Comparable surveys find 40 species in area A and 80 in area 16A, fitting \(S=cA^z\). A restored region has area 4A, but its fitted habitat coefficient is only \(0.75c\). Using this stated model, what is its species richness divided by the original richness in area A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3\sqrt2/4\).
Given: S = cA^z; 40 species in area A; 80 species in area 16A; restored region: area 4A, coefficient 0.75c.
Formula/Principle: Take the ratio of the two surveys to find z.
Step 1: 80/40 = (16A/A)^z, so 2 = 16^z and z = 1/4.
Step 2: Original richness in area A: S₀ = cA^(1/4).
Step 3: Restored region: S = 0.75c(4A)^(1/4) = 0.75 × 4^(1/4) × cA^(1/4) = 0.75√2 × S₀.
Step 4: S/S₀ = 3√2/4 ≈ 1.06.
Why: Species richness rises with area, but slowly: with z = 1/4, a sixteen-fold area only doubles the number of species. The poorer habitat (smaller c) nearly cancels the gain from the four-fold area.
Why not the others: (A) 3/4 ignores the larger area. (C) 3/2 uses z = 1/2. (D) 2 is the ratio for area 16A with the original coefficient.
Key point: log S = log c + z log A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The diagram places two identical polar C–O bonds symmetrically at 180° in CO₂, and two polar O–H bonds at an angle in H₂O. Which molecule has zero net electric dipole in its shown geometry?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) CO₂ only.
Why: A molecular dipole is the vector sum of the bond dipoles. In linear CO₂ the two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. In bent H₂O the two O–H bond dipoles are at about 104.5° to each other and add up to a net dipole along the line bisecting the angle.
Why not the others: (B) Water has a large dipole moment, 1.85 D. (C) CO₂ has zero dipole moment. (D) Only the symmetrical linear molecule cancels.
Key point: Polar bonds + symmetrical shape = non-polar molecule.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Werner formula inference and low-spin electron filling
questions.question: A cobalt compound has empirical composition CoCl₃·4NH₃. Each mole gives one mole of immediate AgCl when treated with excess AgNO₃, and the dissolved complex gives two ions per formula unit. Assume coordinated chloride is not immediately displaced and the octahedral cobalt ion is low spin. Which formula, coordination number and unpaired-electron count fit?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \([\ce{Co(NH3)4Cl2}]\ce{Cl};\ 6;\ 0\).
Given: Composition \(\ce{CoCl3.4NH3}\); 1 mol AgCl per mole with excess \(\ce{AgNO3}\); 2 ions per formula unit; octahedral, low spin.
Formula/Principle: Only chloride outside the coordination sphere is precipitated at once; coordination number = number of donor atoms on the metal.
Step 1: 1 mol AgCl means 1 free \(\ce{Cl-}\); the other two chlorides are ligands: \([\ce{Co(NH3)4Cl2}]\ce{Cl}\).
Step 2: Ions formed: \([\ce{Co(NH3)4Cl2}]^+\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\), which is 2 ions, as observed.
Step 3: Coordination number \(=4+2=6\).
Worked derivation: \[x+4(0)+2(-1)=+1\Rightarrow x=+3;\qquad\ce{Co^3+}:\ 3d^6\ \Rightarrow\ t_{2g}^6e_g^0\ (\text{low spin}),\ \text{unpaired electrons}=0\]
Why: Werner showed that a metal has primary valences, satisfied by ions that can be free, and secondary valences, satisfied by ligands held firmly in the coordination sphere. In a low-spin octahedral d⁶ ion the splitting is large, so all six electrons pair up in the three lower orbitals.
Why not the others: (B) Two free chlorides would give 2 mol of AgCl and three ions. (C) Three free chlorides would give 3 mol of AgCl and four ions. (D) The formula is right, but four unpaired electrons is the high-spin arrangement \(t_{2g}^4e_g^2\).
Key point: Free Cl⁻ is counted by AgNO₃; low-spin d⁶ has no unpaired electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For which of the following substances is the standard enthalpy of formation, Δ_fH°, NOT zero at 298 K?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) C(diamond).
Why: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its reference state, its most stable form at 298 K and 1 bar, is taken as zero. The reference state of carbon is graphite. Diamond is a less stable form, and making it from graphite needs energy: Δ_fH°(diamond) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why not the others: (A) Gaseous O₂ is the reference state of oxygen. (C) Liquid Br₂ is the reference state of bromine. (D) Solid sodium is the reference state of sodium.
Key point: Δ_fH° = 0 only for the most stable form of an element.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ethanoic acid.
Why: The strength of an acid depends on how stable its conjugate base is. In the ethanoate ion the negative charge is shared equally by two oxygen atoms. In the phenoxide ion the charge is spread into the ring, but mainly onto carbon atoms, which is less effective. Hydroxide and ethoxide have no such delocalisation, and in ethoxide the ethyl group pushes electrons towards oxygen. The pK_a values are about 4.8, 10, 15.7 and 16.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanol is the weakest of the four. (B) Water is slightly stronger than ethanol but far weaker than phenol. (D) Phenol is about 10⁵ times weaker than ethanoic acid.
Key point: Carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A Daniell cell is built with Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(1 M) and Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu(s). Immediately after a small amount of Cu²⁺ solution is diluted without changing Zn²⁺ concentration, how does the reaction quotient Q=[Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] change and what is the direction of E relative to its earlier value?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Q rises, E falls.
Why: The cell reaction is Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, with Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. Diluting the copper solution lowers [Cu²⁺], the denominator, so Q rises above 1. By the Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.059/2) log Q, a larger Q gives a smaller E. In terms of Le Chatelier's principle, removing a reactant reduces the driving force of the forward reaction.
Why not the others: (A) Q rises, because its denominator falls. (B) A larger Q lowers E. (C) Q does not fall.
Key point: E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K.
questions.image_alt: A Daniell cell before copper-ion dilution has labelled electrodes, ions and salt bridge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: paired amine class and aromaticity tests
questions.question: An unknown amine gives a positive carbylamine test with CHCl₃ and alcoholic KOH. A separate sample gives a cold, relatively stable diazonium salt with NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5°C, and this couples with alkaline phenol. Which class best fits both observations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Primary aromatic amine.
Why: The carbylamine test (foul-smelling isocyanide with CHCl₃ and alcoholic KOH) is given only by primary amines, aliphatic or aromatic. A diazonium salt that is stable at 0–5 °C and couples with phenol to give a coloured azo dye is formed only by primary aromatic amines. Both results together point to a compound such as aniline.
Why not the others: (B) A primary aliphatic amine gives the carbylamine test, but its diazonium salt decomposes at once to an alcohol and nitrogen. (C) A secondary amine gives no carbylamine test; with nitrous acid it forms a yellow oily nitrosamine. (D) A tertiary amine gives neither test.
Key point: Carbylamine: any 1° amine. Stable diazonium salt and azo dye: 1° aromatic amine.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In acidic solution, 3MnO₄²⁻+4H⁺→2MnO₄⁻+MnO₂+2H₂O is proposed. Is this a disproportionation of Mn(VI), and which products hold its oxidation and reduction outcomes?
options: A) No, Mn remains +6 in all species
B) Yes, Mn(VII) in MnO₄⁻ and Mn(IV) in MnO₂
C) Yes, Mn(V) and Mn(VI) are products
D) No, oxygen alone undergoes redox
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Yes, Mn(VII) in MnO₄⁻ and Mn(IV) in MnO₂.
Why: In manganate, MnO₄²⁻, manganese is +6. In permanganate, MnO₄⁻, it is +7, and in MnO₂ it is +4. The same species is both oxidised (+6 → +7) and reduced (+6 → +4), which is disproportionation. The electrons balance: two Mn lose one electron each and one Mn gains two.
Why not the others: (A) The oxidation number of manganese changes in both products. (C) No Mn(V) is formed, and Mn(VI) is the reactant. (D) Oxygen stays at −2 and hydrogen at +1 throughout.
Key point: Disproportionation: one element in one oxidation state goes both up and down.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For a reaction with activation energy 50 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate ln(k₂/k₁) when temperature rises from 300 K to 330 K; use R=8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and constant activation energy.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.83.
Given: \(E_a=50\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}=50\,000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\); \(T_1=300\ \mathrm K\); \(T_2=330\ \mathrm K\); \(R=8.3\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)\).
Step 1: \(\dfrac1{300}-\dfrac1{330}=\dfrac{30}{99\,000}=3.03\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\).
Step 2: \(\dfrac{E_a}{R}=\dfrac{50\,000}{8.3}=6024\ \mathrm K\).
Worked derivation: \[\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1}=6024\times3.03\times10^{-4}=1.83\]
Why: Raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy, so the rate constant rises. Here k₂/k₁ = e^1.83 ≈ 6.2 for a 30 K rise, in line with the rough rule that the rate doubles for every 10 K.
Why not the others: (A) −1.83 has the wrong sign; the rate constant rises with temperature. (B) 0.18 is ten times too small. (D) 18.3 is ten times too large, which comes from a slip in the powers of ten.
Key point: Keep E_a in J mol⁻¹ and T in kelvin.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol in the presence of a little concentrated H₂SO₄. What is the main organic product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ethyl ethanoate.
Why: A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst to give an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The reaction is reversible; the concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as catalyst and also takes up the water, which pushes the equilibrium towards the ester.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanoic anhydride forms from two molecules of the acid with a strong dehydrating agent such as P₂O₅, not in the presence of an alcohol. (B) Ethoxyethane forms when ethanol alone is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 413 K. (C) Ethanal would need oxidation of ethanol.
Key point: Acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have the same molecular formula, C₃H₈O. Which relationship describes them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Position isomers.
Why: Both compounds are alcohols with the same three-carbon chain. They differ only in the carbon that carries the –OH group: carbon 1 in propan-1-ol and carbon 2 in propan-2-ol. Isomers that differ in the position of the same functional group are position isomers.
Why not the others: (B) Functional isomers have different functional groups, as propan-1-ol and methoxyethane do. (C) Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation, as about a C=C bond. (D) Optical isomerism needs a chiral carbon; neither compound has one.
Key point: Same group, different position: position isomers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Dimer association inferred from apparent molar mass
questions.question: A solute forms only dimers in a dilute ideal solution. Its apparent molar mass inferred from a colligative measurement is 1.50 times its true monomer molar mass. What fraction of the original monomer units is associated into dimers?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2/3.
Given: \(M_{\text{apparent}}=1.50\,M_{\text{true}}\); association \(\ce{2A <=> A2}\).
Formula/Principle: \(i=\dfrac{M_{\text{true}}}{M_{\text{apparent}}}\); for dimerisation \(i=1-\dfrac\alpha2\).
Step 1: \(i=\dfrac{1}{1.50}=\dfrac23\).
Step 2: Start with 1 mol of A; if a fraction α associates, particles \(=(1-\alpha)+\dfrac\alpha2=1-\dfrac\alpha2\).
Worked derivation: \[1-\frac\alpha2=\frac23\Rightarrow\alpha=\frac23\]
Why: Colligative properties count particles. Association reduces the number of particles, so the property is smaller than expected and the molar mass calculated from it is too high. Complete dimerisation would double the apparent molar mass; a factor of 1.5 means part of the solute is associated.
Why not the others: (A) 1/3 is 1 − i, without the factor of two. (C) 1 (complete association) would give an apparent molar mass of twice the true value. (D) 4/3 is greater than 1, which is impossible for a fraction.
Key point: Association: i < 1 and M(apparent) > M(true).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Oxygen allocation across two sulfur-oxidation stages
questions.question: A diagram represents 3 mol sulfur atoms and 4 mol O₂ molecules. Sulfur is converted through \(\ce{S + O2 -> SO2}\) and \(\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}\). The two stages may be allocated to maximise SO₃ with no other reactions. What is the greatest possible SO₃ amount?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8/3 mol.
Given: 3 mol S; 4 mol \(\ce{O2}\); \(\ce{S + O2 -> SO2}\); \(\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}\).
Formula/Principle: Each mole of \(\ce{SO3}\) needs 1 mol S and 1.5 mol \(\ce{O2}\) in all.
Step 1: Let x mol of S be burnt: it uses x mol \(\ce{O2}\) and gives x mol \(\ce{SO2}\).
Step 2: \(\ce{O2}\) left \(=4-x\); it can oxidise \(2(4-x)\) mol \(\ce{SO2}\).
Step 3: \(n(\ce{SO3})\) is the smaller of x and \(8-2x\); it is greatest when \(x=8-2x\).
Worked derivation: \[x=\frac83\ \mathrm{mol};\qquad n(\ce{SO3})=\frac83\ \mathrm{mol};\qquad\ce{O2}\ \text{used}=\frac83\times\frac32=4\ \mathrm{mol}\]
Why: Oxygen is the limiting reagent for making SO₃: 3 mol of S would need 4.5 mol of O₂. If all 3 mol of S is burnt first, only 1 mol of O₂ remains and only 2 mol of SO₃ can form. Leaving 1/3 mol of sulfur unburnt saves oxygen for the second stage.
Why not the others: (A) 3 mol would need 4.5 mol of O₂. (B) 2 mol is the result of burning all the sulfur first. (D) 4 mol would need 4 mol of sulfur and 6 mol of O₂.
Key point: SO₃ = (2/3) × moles of O₂ when oxygen is limiting.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.sub_topic: successive ionisation-energy jump and valence group
questions.question: An element has successive ionisation energies I₁=580, I₂=1817, I₃=2745 and I₄=11578 kJ mol⁻¹. Which number of valence electrons and main-group number are consistent with the sharp jump?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Three; group 13.
Why: Successive ionisation energies rise steadily while electrons are removed from the same shell, and jump sharply when an electron must be taken from an inner, complete shell. Here I₂/I₁ and I₃/I₂ are about 3 and 1.5, but I₄/I₃ is more than 4. Three electrons are removed fairly easily and the fourth is not, so there are three valence electrons. The values are those of aluminium.
Why not the others: (A) One valence electron would put the big jump between I₁ and I₂. (C) Two would put it between I₂ and I₃. (D) Four would put it between I₄ and I₅.
Key point: The large jump comes after the last valence electron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Keratin.
Why: In fibrous proteins the polypeptide chains lie side by side and are held together by hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds, giving fibres that are insoluble in water. Keratin of hair, wool and nails and myosin of muscle are examples. In globular proteins the chain folds into a compact, roughly spherical shape that is usually soluble in water.
Why not the others: (A) Insulin is a small globular protein hormone. (B) Albumin is a soluble globular protein. (D) Haemoglobin is a globular protein of four subunits.
Key point: Fibrous: structural, insoluble. Globular: soluble, enzymes, hormones, carriers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: pH of a very dilute strong acid
questions.question: What is the approximate pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M solution of HCl at 298 K?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6.98.
Given: \([\ce{HCl}]=1.0\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm M\); \(K_w=1.0\times10^{-14}\) at 298 K.
Formula/Principle: Total \([\ce{H+}]\) = H⁺ from the acid + H⁺ from water; \([\ce{H+}][\ce{OH-}]=K_w\).
Step 1: Let water supply x mol L⁻¹ of \(\ce{H+}\) and \(\ce{OH-}\): \((10^{-8}+x)\,x=10^{-14}\).
Step 2: \(x^2+10^{-8}x-10^{-14}=0\Rightarrow x=9.5\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm M\).
Step 3: \([\ce{H+}]=1.0\times10^{-8}+9.5\times10^{-8}=1.05\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm M\).
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{pH}=-\log(1.05\times10^{-7})=7-0.02=6.98\]
Why: The acid is so dilute that water itself supplies most of the hydrogen ions, so its ionisation cannot be ignored. The solution of an acid must be acidic, however dilute, so the pH must be just below 7.
Why not the others: (A) 8.0 comes from −log(10⁻⁸) and would make an acid solution alkaline. (B) 7.0 ignores the acid altogether. (C) 6.0 has no basis; it would need [H⁺] = 10⁻⁶ M.
Key point: Below about 10⁻⁶ M, include the H⁺ from water.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The circle (x−2)²+(y+1)²=9 touches which of the following horizontal lines?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) y=2.
Given: \((x-2)^2+(y+1)^2=9\Rightarrow\text{centre }(2,-1),\ r=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{horizontal tangents}:\ y=y_c\pm r\)
Step 1: \(y=-1+3=2,\quad y=-1-3=-4\)
Worked derivation: \[y=2\ \ (\text{touches at }(2,2))\]
Check: \[y=2:\ (x-2)^2+9=9\Rightarrow x=2\ (\text{one point})\]
Why: \(\text{tangent}\iff\text{distance from the centre}=r\)
Why not the others: (B) \(y=0:\ d=1<3\); (C) \(y=-1:\ d=0<3\); (D) \(y=4:\ d=5>3\).
Key point: \(\text{distance from centre to line}=\text{radius}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: On the closed interval [−1,2], what is the maximum of f(x)=x⁴−2x²?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8.
Given: \(f(x)=x^4-2x^2,\quad x\in[-1,2]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{compare }f\text{ at the critical points and the endpoints}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=4x^3-4x=4x(x-1)(x+1)=0\Rightarrow x=-1,\ 0,\ 1\)
Step 2: \(f(-1)=-1,\quad f(0)=0,\quad f(1)=-1,\quad f(2)=16-8=8\)
Worked derivation: \[\max f=f(2)=8\]
Check: \[f'(x)>0\ \text{for}\ x>1\Rightarrow f\ \text{increasing on}\ [1,2]\]
Why: \(\text{a continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0=f(0)\) (local maximum only); (B) \(-1=f(\pm1)\) (minimum); (C) \(1\ne f(x)\ \text{at any candidate point}\).
Key point: \(\text{always test the endpoints}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A curve is given implicitly by x²y+y³=2. At its point (1,1), what is the tangent slope?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −1/2.
Given: \(x^2y+y^3=2,\quad P=(1,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{implicit differentiation}\)
Step 1: \(2xy+x^2y'+3y^2y'=0\)
Step 2: \(y'=-\dfrac{2xy}{x^2+3y^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y'(1,1)=-\frac{2}{1+3}=-\frac12\]
Check: \[1^2(1)+1^3=2\]
Why: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-2\) (denominator omitted); (B) \(+\tfrac12\) (sign); (C) \(0\ne-\tfrac12\).
Key point: \(y'=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_y}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹ dx/[(x+1)²(x+2)].
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2−ln(4/3).
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2(x+2)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2(x+2)}=\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2}+\dfrac{C}{x+2}\)
Step 1: \(1=A(x+1)(x+2)+B(x+2)+C(x+1)^2\)
Step 2: \(x=-1:\ B=1;\quad x=-2:\ C=1;\quad x^2:\ A+C=0\Rightarrow A=-1\)
Step 3: \(I=\left[-\ln(x+1)-\dfrac{1}{x+1}+\ln(x+2)\right]_0^1\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\left(-\ln2-\frac12+\ln3\right)-\left(0-1+\ln2\right)=\frac12+\ln\frac34=\frac12-\ln\frac43\approx0.212\]
Check: \[0<\frac{1}{(x+1)^2(x+2)}\le\frac12\ \text{on}\ [0,1];\quad0<0.212<0.5\]
Why: \(\text{repeated linear factor}\Rightarrow\text{terms in}\ \dfrac{1}{x+1}\ \text{and}\ \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\ln\tfrac43\) (\(B\) term omitted, sign reversed); (C) \(\tfrac12+\ln\tfrac43\) (sign of the logarithm); (D) \(\tfrac12\) (logarithms omitted).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2}=-\frac{1}{x+1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Inverse domain and branch of a logarithmic composition
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=\ln(x^2-1)\) for \(x>1\), and let g be its inverse. Which pair gives \(g(\ln3)\) and the domain of g?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2;\ \mathbb R\).
Given: \(f(x)=\ln(x^2-1),\ x>1;\quad g=f^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(g(y)=x\iff f(x)=y;\quad\text{domain of }g=\text{range of }f\)
Step 1: \(\ln(x^2-1)=\ln3\Rightarrow x^2=4\Rightarrow x=2\ \ (x>1)\)
Step 2: \(x\to1^+:\ f\to-\infty;\quad x\to\infty:\ f\to+\infty\Rightarrow\text{range}=\mathbb R\)
Worked derivation: \[g(\ln3)=2;\qquad\text{domain of }g=\mathbb R\]
Check: \[g(y)=\sqrt{e^y+1}\ \text{is defined for all real}\ y\]
Why: \(f\ \text{is increasing on}\ (1,\infty)\Rightarrow\text{one-one}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-2\notin(1,\infty)\); (B) \(\text{range of }f=\mathbb R,\ \text{not}\ (0,\infty)\); (D) \(f(\sqrt2)=\ln1=0\ne\ln3\).
Key point: \(\text{domain of }f^{-1}=\text{range of }f\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Relations and functions: inverse functions; logarithmic functions

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Vectors a=(1,1,0) and b=(1,−1,2) are viewed by an observer on the positive z-axis looking toward the origin. Which pair gives a×b and whether its z-component points into or out of the screen?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (2,−2,−2), into the screen.
Given: \(\mathbf a=(1,1,0),\quad\mathbf b=(1,-1,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\)
Step 1: \(a_2b_3-a_3b_2=2-0=2\)
Step 2: \(a_3b_1-a_1b_3=0-2=-2\)
Step 3: \(a_1b_2-a_2b_1=-1-1=-2\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=(2,-2,-2);\qquad z<0\Rightarrow\text{away from the observer on }+z\ (\text{into the screen})\]
Check: \[\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=2-2+0=0;\quad\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=2+2-4=0\]
Why: \(\text{the observer looks along }-z;\ \text{a vector with }z<0\ \text{points away from the observer}\)
Why not the others: (A) \((-2,2,2)=\mathbf b\times\mathbf a\); (B) \(z=+2\) (sign of the third component); (C) \(z=0\ne-2\).
Key point: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\perp\mathbf a,\ \mathbf b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Matrix inverse with a trace constraint
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\), with real t. For which t does A have an inverse whose trace (sum of diagonal entries) is 1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1\pm\sqrt2\).
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det A}\begin{pmatrix}t&-1\\-1&t\end{pmatrix},\quad\det A=t^2-1\ne0\)
Step 1: \(\operatorname{tr}A^{-1}=\dfrac{2t}{t^2-1}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{2t}{t^2-1}=1\Rightarrow t^2-2t-1=0\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4+4}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt2\]
Check: \[t=1+\sqrt2:\ t^2-1=2+2\sqrt2=2t\]
Why: \(t=\pm1\ \text{excluded}\ (\det A=0)\)
Why not the others: (B) \(t=1:\ \det A=0\); (C) \(t=\pm1:\ \det A=0\); (D) \(t=-1:\ \det A=0\).
Key point: \(\operatorname{tr}A^{-1}=\dfrac{\operatorname{tr}A}{\det A}\ \text{for}\ 2\times2\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Matrices and determinants: inverse and determinant

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Two different tickets are drawn without replacement from five numbered 1 to 5, with unordered pairs equally likely. Given that their product is even, what is the probability both tickets are even?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/7.
Given: \(\text{tickets }1,\dots,5;\ \text{two drawn without replacement};\ \text{product even}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A|B)=\dfrac{n(A\cap B)}{n(B)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{all pairs}:\ \dbinom52=10\)
Step 2: \(\text{product odd}\iff\text{both odd}:\ \dbinom32=3\Rightarrow n(B)=10-3=7\)
Step 3: \(\text{both even}:\ \{2,4\}\Rightarrow n(A\cap B)=1\)
Worked derivation: \[P=\frac17\]
Check: \[7=\binom21\binom31+\binom22=6+1\]
Why: \(\text{both even}\subset\text{product even}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac1{10}\) (condition ignored); (C) \(\tfrac25\); (D) \(\tfrac12\).
Key point: \(\text{reduce the sample space to the given event}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many nonempty multisets of size 4 can be chosen from 3 available types if supply is unlimited?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 15.
Given: \(\text{multisets of size }4\ \text{from }3\ \text{types}\)
Formula/Principle: \(x_1+x_2+x_3=4,\ x_i\ge0:\ \dbinom{n+r-1}{r-1}\)
Step 1: \(n=4,\ r=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\binom{4+3-1}{3-1}=\binom62=15\]
Check: \[(4,0,0):3;\ (3,1,0):6;\ (2,2,0):3;\ (2,1,1):3;\quad3+6+3+3=15\]
Why: \(\text{stars and bars: 4 stars, 2 bars}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4\times3=12\); (B) \(\dbinom53=10\); (D) \(15-1=14\).
Key point: \(\text{selections with repetition}=\dbinom{n+r-1}{r-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let p be a positive integer. In the expansion of (x^p+x⁻²)⁶, the coefficient of the term independent of x is 15. What is the sum of all possible p?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5.
Given: \(\left(x^p+x^{-2}\right)^6,\ p\in\mathbb Z^+;\quad\text{constant term}=15\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{k+1}=\dbinom6kx^{p(6-k)}x^{-2k}\)
Step 1: \(\text{constant}:\ p(6-k)=2k\)
Step 2: \(\dbinom6k=15\Rightarrow k=2\ \text{or}\ k=4\)
Step 3: \(k=2:\ 4p=4\Rightarrow p=1;\quad k=4:\ 2p=8\Rightarrow p=4\)
Worked derivation: \[1+4=5\]
Check: \[p=1:\ \left(x+x^{-2}\right)^6,\ k=2:\ x^4x^{-4}=1;\quad p=4:\ k=4:\ x^8x^{-8}=1\]
Why: \(\dbinom62=\dbinom64=15\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\) (\(k=4\) omitted); (B) \(4\) (\(k=2\) omitted); (C) \(6\ne5\).
Key point: \(\dbinom nk=\dbinom n{n-k}\ \text{gives two cases}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Positive GP terms from sum and product
questions.question: Three positive, strictly increasing numbers a, b and c form a geometric progression. Their sum is 13 and their product is 27. What is the sum of the first five terms of that progression beginning with a?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 121.
Given: \(a<b<c\ \text{in GP},\ a,b,c>0;\quad a+b+c=13;\quad abc=27\)
Formula/Principle: \(a=\dfrac br,\ c=br\Rightarrow abc=b^3\)
Step 1: \(b^3=27\Rightarrow b=3\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac3r+3+3r=13\Rightarrow3r^2-10r+3=0\Rightarrow r=3\ \text{or}\ \tfrac13\)
Step 3: \(\text{increasing}\Rightarrow r=3,\ a=1\)
Worked derivation: \[S_5=\frac{3^5-1}{3-1}=\frac{242}{2}=121\]
Check: \[1+3+9=13,\quad1\times3\times9=27;\quad1+3+9+27+81=121\]
Why: \(\text{writing the terms as}\ \tfrac br,\ b,\ br\ \text{makes the product}\ b^3\)
Why not the others: (B) \(40=S_4\); (C) \(120=S_5-1\); (D) \(243=3^5\).
Key point: \(S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and series: geometric progression and finite sum

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Polynomials x²−3x+2 and x²−kx+4 share one real root. What is the sum of all real possible k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 9.
Given: \(x^2-3x+2=0,\quad x^2-kx+4=0\ \text{share a real root}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{substitute each root of the first into the second}\)
Step 1: \(x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)\Rightarrow x=1,\ 2\)
Step 2: \(x=1:\ 1-k+4=0\Rightarrow k=5\)
Step 3: \(x=2:\ 4-2k+4=0\Rightarrow k=4\)
Worked derivation: \[5+4=9\]
Check: \[k=5:\ (x-1)(x-4);\qquad k=4:\ (x-2)^2\]
Why: \(\text{a common root satisfies both equations}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(5\) (\(k=4\) omitted); (C) \(7\ne9\); (D) \(6\ne9\).
Key point: \(\text{test each root of the factorable equation}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Removing one observation from a mean
questions.question: Five numbers have mean 8. One number is removed and the mean of the remaining four is 7. Which number was removed?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 12.
Given: \(n=5,\ \bar x=8;\quad\text{after removal}:\ n=4,\ \bar x=7\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\sum x=n\bar x\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\sum_5x=5\times8=40\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\sum_4x=4\times7=28\)
Worked derivation: \[x_{\text{removed}}=40-28=12\]
Check: \[\frac{28+12}{5}=8\]
Why: \(\text{the mean fell}\Rightarrow\text{the removed number exceeded the mean}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(8-7=1\); (B) \(8\ \text{would leave the mean unchanged}\); (D) \(8+7=15\).
Key point: \(\text{work with totals, not means}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating factor of a linear differential equation
questions.question: What is the integrating factor of the differential equation y′+y tan x=sec x, for 0<x<π/2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) sec x.
Given: \(y'+y\tan x=\sec x,\quad0<x<\tfrac\pi2\)
Formula/Principle: \(y'+P(x)y=Q(x):\ \text{IF}=e^{\int P\,dx}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln\cos x=\ln\sec x\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{IF}=e^{\ln\sec x}=\sec x\]
Check: \[(y\sec x)'=y'\sec x+y\sec x\tan x=\sec x\,(y'+y\tan x)=\sec^2x\Rightarrow y\sec x=\tan x+C\]
Why: \(\text{the IF turns the left side into an exact derivative}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\cos x=e^{-\int\tan x\,dx}\); (B) \(\tan x=P(x)\); (D) \(e^{\tan x}=e^{P}\) (not integrated).
Key point: \(\text{IF}=e^{\int P\,dx}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate limₓ→₀ (e^(2x)−1−2x)/x².
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.
Given: \(L=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1-2x}{x^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(e^u=1+u+\dfrac{u^2}{2}+\dots\)
Step 1: \(e^{2x}=1+2x+\dfrac{(2x)^2}{2}+\dfrac{(2x)^3}{6}+\dots\)
Step 2: \(e^{2x}-1-2x=2x^2+\dfrac43x^3+\dots\)
Worked derivation: \[L=\lim_{x\to0}\left(2+\frac43x+\dots\right)=2\]
Check: \[\text{L'Hôpital twice}:\ \frac{2e^{2x}-2}{2x}\to\frac{4e^{2x}}{2}=2\]
Why: \(\text{the terms }1\text{ and }2x\text{ cancel}\Rightarrow\text{the }x^2\text{ term decides}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(1\) (\(\tfrac{u^2}{2}\) with \(u=x\)); (C) \(4\) (\(\tfrac12\) omitted); (D) \(0\ne2\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{ax}-1-ax}{x^2}=\frac{a^2}{2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.sub_topic: Distance fallen in the nth second
questions.question: A stone is dropped from rest from a high tower. Taking g=10 m s⁻², how far does it fall during the third second of its motion?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 25 m.
Given: \(u=0,\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(s(t)=\tfrac12gt^2,\quad s_{n\text{th}}=s(n)-s(n-1)\)
Step 1: \(s(3)=\tfrac12(10)(9)=45\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(s(2)=\tfrac12(10)(4)=20\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[s_{3\text{rd}}=45-20=25\ \mathrm m\]
Check: \[s_n=\frac g2(2n-1)=5\times5=25\ \mathrm m;\quad5:15:25=1:3:5\]
Why: \(\text{distances in successive seconds are in the ratio }1:3:5\)
Why not the others: (A) \(15\ \mathrm m\) (second second); (C) \(30\ \mathrm m=v(3)\times1\) (numerically \(gt\)); (D) \(45\ \mathrm m=s(3)\) (total).
Key point: \(s_n=u+\dfrac a2(2n-1)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A block is released from rest on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g=10 m s⁻², how long does it take to slide 10 m along the plane?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 s.
Given: \(\theta=30^\circ,\quad u=0,\quad s=10\ \mathrm m,\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\quad\text{smooth}\)
Formula/Principle: \(a=g\sin\theta,\quad s=\tfrac12at^2\)
Step 1: \(a=10\times\tfrac12=5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Step 2: \(t^2=\dfrac{2s}{a}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4\ \mathrm{s^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[t=2\ \mathrm s\]
Check: \[v=at=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\quad\tfrac12v^2=50=g(s\sin\theta)=10\times5\]
Why: \(\text{only the component of gravity along the plane accelerates the block}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\ \mathrm s:\ s=2.5\ \mathrm m\); (B) \(\sqrt2\ \mathrm s\) (\(a=g\)); (D) \(4\ \mathrm s=t^2\) (root not taken).
Key point: \(a=g\sin\theta\ \text{on a smooth incline}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 2 kg particle enters x=0 at 2 m s⁻¹. The pictured force along its motion is F(x)=2x N from 0 to 2 m, then 4 N from 2 to 3 m. With no other work, what speed does it have at x=3 m?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2√3 m s⁻¹.
Given: \(m=2\ \mathrm{kg},\quad v_0=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\quad F=2x\ \mathrm N\ (0\text{–}2\ \mathrm m),\quad F=4\ \mathrm N\ (2\text{–}3\ \mathrm m)\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\displaystyle\int F\,dx=\Delta K\)
Step 1: \(W_1=\displaystyle\int_0^22x\,dx=4\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(W_2=4\times1=4\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(K_f=\tfrac12(2)(2)^2+8=12\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[v=\sqrt{\frac{2K_f}{m}}=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[\text{area under the graph}:\ \tfrac12(2)(4)+4(1)=8\ \mathrm J\]
Why: \(\text{work}=\text{area under the }F\text{–}x\text{ graph}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=v_0\); (B) \(\sqrt8\) (initial kinetic energy omitted); (C) \(4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}:\ K=16\ \mathrm J\ne12\ \mathrm J\).
Key point: \(\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mv_0^2=\displaystyle\int F\,dx\)
questions.image_alt: A force-position curve rises linearly then has a constant second segment.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: A uniform solid disk rolls without slipping down from rest through vertical height h. What fraction of its final kinetic energy is rotational about its centre?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1/3.
Given: \(\text{uniform solid disc},\ I=\tfrac12MR^2,\ \text{rolling without slipping}\)
Formula/Principle: \(K=\tfrac12Mv^2+\tfrac12I\omega^2,\quad v=\omega R\)
Step 1: \(K_{\text{rot}}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12MR^2\cdot\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac14Mv^2\)
Step 2: \(K=\tfrac12Mv^2+\tfrac14Mv^2=\tfrac34Mv^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{K_{\text{rot}}}{K}=\frac{1/4}{3/4}=\frac13\]
Check: \[Mgh=\tfrac34Mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\tfrac43gh}<\sqrt{2gh}\]
Why: \(\text{the fraction depends only on}\ \dfrac{I}{MR^2}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac14\) (\(K_{\text{rot}}/Mv^2\)); (C) \(\tfrac12\) (ring); (D) \(\tfrac23\) (translational fraction).
Key point: \(\dfrac{K_{\text{rot}}}{K}=\dfrac{k^2}{k^2+R^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: At what height above the Earth's surface is the acceleration due to gravity one quarter of its value at the surface? (R is the Earth's radius.)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) R.
Given: \(g(h)=\dfrac{g}{4}\)
Formula/Principle: \(g(h)=\dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^2}=g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2\)
Step 1: \(\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2=\dfrac14\Rightarrow\dfrac{R}{R+h}=\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[R+h=2R\Rightarrow h=R\]
Check: \[r=2R:\ g\propto\frac{1}{r^2}\Rightarrow\frac g4\]
Why: \(\text{distance is measured from the centre of the Earth}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(h=\tfrac R2:\ g\left(\tfrac23\right)^2=\tfrac49g\); (C) \(h=2R:\ \tfrac g9\); (D) \(h=4R:\ \tfrac g{25}\).
Key point: \(g\propto\dfrac{1}{(R+h)^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A uniform block of density 600 kg m⁻³ floats upright in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. What fraction of its height is submerged at equilibrium?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.6.
Given: \(\rho_b=600\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},\quad\rho_w=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{weight}=\text{buoyant force}:\ \rho_bVg=\rho_wV_{\text{sub}}g\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V}=\dfrac{\rho_b}{\rho_w}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{h_{\text{sub}}}{h}=\frac{600}{1000}=0.6\]
Check: \[\rho_b<\rho_w\Rightarrow\text{floats};\quad0<0.6<1\]
Why: \(\text{uniform upright block}\Rightarrow\text{volume fraction}=\text{height fraction}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0.4\) (fraction above water); (B) \(0.5\ne0.6\); (D) \(1.0\) (\(\rho_b=\rho_w\)).
Key point: \(\text{fraction submerged}=\dfrac{\rho_{\text{body}}}{\rho_{\text{fluid}}}\)
questions.image_alt: A partly immersed uniform block has its density and the water density labelled.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: First law for expansion at constant pressure
questions.question: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ while absorbing 500 J of heat. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 300 J.
Given: \(p=2.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa},\quad V_1=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},\quad V_2=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},\quad Q=+500\ \mathrm J\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=p\,\Delta V,\quad\Delta U=Q-W\)
Step 1: \(W=2.0\times10^{5}\times1.0\times10^{-3}=200\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=500-200=300\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\mathrm{Pa\cdot m^3}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}\cdot m^3}=\mathrm J\]
Why: \(\text{part of the heat does work; the rest raises the internal energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(500+200=700\ \mathrm J\) (sign of \(W\)); (B) \(200\ \mathrm J=W\); (C) \(500\ \mathrm J=Q\).
Key point: \(\Delta U=Q-p\,\Delta V\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: Two identical positive charges +q are fixed at x=−a and x=+a. At which finite x on their joining axis is the net electric field zero?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) x=0.
Given: \(+q\ \text{at}\ x=-a,\quad+q\ \text{at}\ x=+a\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2},\ \text{directed away from a positive charge}\)
Step 1: \(-a<x<a:\ E=\dfrac{kq}{(x+a)^2}-\dfrac{kq}{(a-x)^2}\)
Step 2: \(E=0\Rightarrow(x+a)^2=(a-x)^2\Rightarrow x=0\)
Worked derivation: \[x=0\]
Check: \[|x|>a:\ \text{both fields point the same way}\Rightarrow E\ne0\]
Why: \(\text{equal like charges}\Rightarrow\text{null point at the midpoint}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=-2a:\ \text{both fields along}\ -x\); (C) \(x=2a:\ \text{both fields along}\ +x\); (D) \(x=0\ \text{is a finite null point}\).
Key point: \(\text{like charges: null point between them}\)
questions.image_alt: Equal positive charges lie symmetrically on the x-axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Capacitance when geometry and dielectric change
questions.question: A parallel-plate air capacitor has capacitance C. Its plate area is doubled, its plate separation is doubled, and the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of constant 2. What is the new capacitance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2C.
Given: \(C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d};\quad A\to2A,\ d\to2d,\ K=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(C'=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A'}{d'}\)
Step 1: \(C'=\dfrac{2\,\varepsilon_0(2A)}{2d}\)
Worked derivation: \[C'=2\,\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}=2C\]
Check: \[\text{area}\times2,\ \text{separation}\times\tfrac12,\ \text{dielectric}\times2:\ 2\times\tfrac12\times2=2\]
Why: \(C\propto\dfrac{KA}{d}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(C\) (dielectric omitted); (C) \(4C\) (separation omitted); (D) \(\dfrac C2\) (only the separation counted).
Key point: \(C=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.question: A charge +q moves at v=2 m s⁻¹ along +x in a magnetic field B=3 T along +y. What is magnetic-force direction and magnitude, for q=1 C?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) +z, 6 N.
Given: \(q=+1\ \mathrm C,\quad\mathbf v=2\,\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad\mathbf B=3\,\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf F=q\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\)
Step 1: \(\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf F=(1)(2)(3)\,\hat{\mathbf z}=6\,\hat{\mathbf z}\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=0,\quad\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf B=0\]
Why: \(\mathbf v\perp\mathbf B\Rightarrow F=qvB\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-\hat{\mathbf z}\) (\(\mathbf B\times\mathbf v\)); (B) \(3\ \mathrm N\) (\(v\) omitted); (D) \(-\hat{\mathbf y}\parallel\mathbf B\).
Key point: \(\mathbf F\perp\mathbf v\ \text{and}\ \mathbf F\perp\mathbf B\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Peak emf of an AC generator
questions.question: A coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.010 m², rotates at 50 rad s⁻¹ in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T about an axis perpendicular to the field. What is the peak emf induced?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10 V.
Given: \(N=100,\quad A=0.010\ \mathrm{m^2},\quad\omega=50\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\quad B=0.20\ \mathrm T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Phi=NBA\cos\omega t,\quad\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega\)
Worked derivation: \[\varepsilon_0=100\times0.20\times0.010\times50=10\ \mathrm V\]
Check: \[\mathrm{T\,m^2\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{Wb\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm V\]
Why: \(\text{the emf is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0.10\ \mathrm V\) (\(N\) omitted); (B) \(1.0\ \mathrm V\); (C) \(5.0\ \mathrm V\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A convex lens with f=10 cm has an object 5 cm in front of it. Which image is formed, using Cartesian signs with light left to right?
options: A) Virtual upright on object side, 10 cm from lens
B) Real inverted on far side, 10 cm
C) Virtual inverted on far side, 5 cm
D) Real upright on object side, 5 cm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Virtual upright on object side, 10 cm from lens.
Given: \(f=+10\ \mathrm{cm},\quad u=-5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f,\quad m=\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1{10}+\dfrac{1}{-5}=-\dfrac1{10}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=-10\ \mathrm{cm};\qquad m=\frac{-10}{-5}=+2\]
Check: \[v<0\Rightarrow\text{same side as the object (virtual)};\quad m>0\Rightarrow\text{upright}\]
Why: \(|u|<f\Rightarrow\text{magnifying-glass case}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(v=+10\ \mathrm{cm}\) (sign); (C) \(\text{a virtual image of a real object is upright}\); (D) \(\text{a real image of a real object is inverted}\).
Key point: \(\text{object inside the focus of a convex lens}\Rightarrow\text{virtual, upright, magnified}\)
questions.image_alt: A converging lens has an object inside its left focal distance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In a single-slit Fraunhofer setup, slit width is halved while wavelength and screen distance remain fixed. What happens to the central maximum's linear width?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Doubles.
Given: \(a\to\dfrac a2,\quad\lambda,\ D\ \text{fixed}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{first minima}:\ a\sin\theta=\pm\lambda;\quad\text{width}=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\)
Step 1: \(w'=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a/2}\)
Worked derivation: \[w'=2\cdot\frac{2\lambda D}{a}=2w\]
Check: \[a\to\infty:\ w\to0\ \ (\text{geometrical shadow})\]
Why: \(\text{a narrower slit spreads the light more}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(w\propto\dfrac1a,\ \text{not}\ a\); (C) \(w\propto\dfrac1a,\ \text{not}\ \dfrac1{a^2}\); (D) \(w\ \text{depends on}\ a\).
Key point: \(\text{central width}=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Which spectral feature distinguishes a hot dilute atomic gas from a hot dense source viewed through a dispersing prism?
options: A) Continuous spectrum in all cases
B) No radiation from dilute gas
C) Bright discrete emission lines at characteristic wavelengths
D) Only a single universal line for all elements
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bright discrete emission lines at characteristic wavelengths.
Given: \(\text{hot dilute atomic gas}\)
Formula/Principle: \(hf=E_i-E_f\)
Step 1: \(\text{isolated atoms}\Rightarrow\text{discrete energy levels}\ E_n\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda=\frac{hc}{E_i-E_f}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{only certain wavelengths (line spectrum)}\]
Check: \[\text{hydrogen}:\ \lambda_{3\to2}=\frac{1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{1.89\ \mathrm{eV}}=656\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Why: \(\text{dense hot source}\Rightarrow\text{levels broadened into bands}\Rightarrow\text{continuous spectrum}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{continuous only for dense sources}\); (B) \(\text{a hot dilute gas does emit}\); (D) \(E_n\ \text{differ from element to element}\).
Key point: \(\text{line spectrum}=\text{fingerprint of an element}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Infer half-life then apply source-only attenuation and background
questions.question: A detector reads 900 counts min⁻¹ at t=0 and 500 counts min⁻¹ at t=4 h from one radioactive source plus a constant electronic background of 100 counts min⁻¹. Immediately before the reading at t=12 h, a screen is inserted that halves detected source events but does not change the electronic background. What total rate is then expected?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 150 counts min⁻¹.
Given: \(R(0)=900,\ R(4\ \mathrm h)=500\ \text{counts min}^{-1};\quad\text{background }b=100;\quad\text{screen halves source counts at }12\ \mathrm h\)
Formula/Principle: \(S(t)=S_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T},\quad R=S+b\)
Step 1: \(S(0)=900-100=800,\quad S(4)=500-100=400\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{S(4)}{S(0)}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow T=4\ \mathrm h\)
Step 3: \(S(12)=800\left(\tfrac12\right)^3=100\)
Step 4: \(\text{with screen}:\ \tfrac12\times100=50\)
Worked derivation: \[R=50+100=150\ \text{counts min}^{-1}\]
Check: \[\text{without the screen}:\ 100+100=200\]
Why: \(\text{the background does not decay and is not screened}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(100\) (background only); (B) \(200\) (screen omitted); (C) \(250\ne150\).
Key point: \(\text{subtract the background before using the decay law}\)
